cards.text: This one's labeled a song for the Sabbath day, and the songwriter skips the warmup. Right out of the gate he says it is good to praise the LORD and to sing praises to His name, O Most High. Not "fine," not "if you've got a minute," but GOOD.

cards.question: The songwriter wants praise that covers the whole day, proclaiming the LORD's loving devotion in the ___ and His faithfulness at ___.
This is a song, so it's not going out with no music behind it. What instruments does the songwriter want playing along?

answers.text: The ten-stringed harp and the lyre

cards.question: Then the songwriter gives the reason behind all this singing. He says the LORD has made him glad. By what?
The songwriter can't get over the LORD. True or false: he says the LORD's works are great and His thoughts are deep.

cards.text: Then he says there's something a senseless man doesn't know and a fool doesn't understand. And it's about the wicked.

cards.question: The wicked sprout like grass, and all evildoers flourish. But the songwriter says they will be forever ___.

cards.text: Then, right in the middle of the song, comes the shortest line of all: "But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!" The wicked sprout like grass, but the LORD is up there FOREVER.

cards.question: True or false: the songwriter says the LORD's enemies will come out on top in the end.

cards.text: Then it gets personal: the LORD has exalted the songwriter's horn like that of a wild ox, and he's been anointed with fine oil. Not a petting zoo goat, friend, a WILD OX.

cards.question: The songwriter has been singing about the LORD's enemies perishing. What does he say his own eyes see?

cards.text: Now the song comes back to the plant world. Remember, the wicked sprouted like grass, which is basically a viral video: EVERYWHERE for a week, then nobody can even remember what it was.

cards.question: If the wicked are like grass, what does the songwriter say the righteous will flourish like?

cards.text: A palm tree, and they'll grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They're planted in the house of the LORD, and they flourish in the courts of our God.

cards.question: True or false: the songwriter says the righteous stop bearing fruit once they reach old age.

cards.text: Nope, in old age they still bear fruit, and they stay healthy and green. My edges went soft and blurry in that junk drawer, friend, so I'm hugging this verse with my WHOLE mustache.

cards.question: The song ends with the righteous still flourishing in old age. What does the songwriter say they'll proclaim?

answers.text: The LORD is upright and is their Rock
Their own strength carried them through
Their good works made them great

findings.problem: The setup ('covers the whole day') lets the baker reason out morning and night. But which word goes with loving devotion and which goes with faithfulness is only the line's wording. A baker who understands the verse can still miss the card by swapping the two words.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The setup line 'The songwriter can't get over the LORD' tells the baker the statement is praise. That rules out False before the baker has to reason about anything.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The question sets up a contrast: the wicked flourish, 'But' they will be forever ___. That contrast rules out both wrong answers, 'honored' and 'remembered', because neither one contrasts with flourishing.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The setup says the songwriter 'has been singing about the LORD's enemies perishing.' That points straight to 'The downfall of his enemies' and rules out 'taking his land' and 'asking for peace'.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: This card goes back to verse 7 ('Remember, the wicked sprouted like grass') after the walkthrough has reached verse 11. It is a recap with a joke attached and doesn't tell any new part of the passage.

Papa Dorin says his edges went soft and blurry 'in that junk drawer.' In his backstory they wore down from years of baking on the Millers' counter, before he was put in the drawer. The line changes his backstory.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The right answer is the only one about the LORD, and it uses Bible words ('upright', 'Rock'). Both wrong answers are about the people's own strength or works, so the right answer stands out by its tone.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
